# Measuring behaviour change with an event-study / difference-in-differences

## Introduction

A common question in Copilot Analytics is *causal*: **did a person's
collaboration behaviour change after they started using Copilot**, or
are heavy users simply different people to begin with? A plain comparison of
users vs non-users cannot separate the two, because adoption is not random.

A **within-person event-study** paired with a **difference-in-differences
(DiD)** design is a standard way to approach this. The design:

* aligns every adopter on their own **event time** (weeks relative to the week
  they adopted Copilot),
* compares adopters against a control group of non-adopters over the same
  calendar weeks,
* absorbs each person's baseline (**person fixed effects**) and every calendar
  week's common shocks (**week fixed effects**), and
* reads the estimate as the *within-person* change in the treated group
  relative to the control group.

Adoption here is **staggered**: people adopt in different weeks. A single
two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) regression can give misleading estimates in that
setting when effects differ by adoption cohort or change over time, because
already-adopted people can end up acting as comparisons for later adopters
(Goodman-Bacon 2021; de Chaisemartin and D'Haultfoeuille 2020). This notebook
therefore uses the **Sun and Abraham (2021) interaction-weighted estimator** as
the primary estimate. It estimates an effect for each adoption cohort and
event week, using never-adopters as the comparison group, then averages those
effects. The naive TWFE event study is kept only as a comparison.

The results are estimates under assumptions (chiefly parallel trends and no
anticipation), and are best read as associations consistent with an effect
rather than proof of one.

Person Query exports do not ship with a clean adoption event, so this notebook
builds a **small seeded simulation** whose column names match a real Person
Query. The downstream modelling code therefore runs on a real export loaded
with `vivainsights::import_query()`, so you swap out the data-generation chunk and
map your outcome columns (shown below). The simulation injects a **clearly-labelled
illustrative effect** so the model has something to recover; this is for
demonstration only and is not a real result.

## Set-up

This example uses **fixest** (a recent version, tested with 0.14.2) for fast
fixed-effects estimation; install it with
`install.packages("fixest")` if you do not already have it.

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)
library(fixest)   # fast fixed-effects estimation (feols, sunab(), i())
```

To run this notebook on your **own** export instead of the simulation, replace
the simulation chunk below with the following, then continue unchanged from the
*"Derive the adoption week"* section:

```{r real-data, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
panel <- vivainsights::import_query("your-person-query.csv")
app_cols <- grep("^Copilot_actions_taken_in", names(panel), value = TRUE)
panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(app_cols), ~ tidyr::replace_na(.x, 0))) %>%
  mutate(Total_Copilot_actions_taken = rowSums(across(all_of(app_cols))))
# choose the outcome column(s) to model, e.g. Collaboration_hours, Chat_hours,
# Emails_sent -- these are standard Person Query columns.
```

## Simulate a Person-Query-shaped panel

The block below creates a weekly panel with the same shape as a Person Query:
one row per `PersonId` x `MetricDate`, a `Total_Copilot_actions_taken` column,
and a few collaboration outcomes (`Collaboration_hours`, `Chat_hours`,
`Emails_sent`). Treated people adopt Copilot at a **staggered** week; control
people never adopt. We add person baselines, calendar-week seasonality, and
noise so the panel looks realistic.

> **Replace this chunk for real data.** Load your export with
> `vivainsights::import_query()` and derive the adoption week from the first week
> of non-zero Copilot actions (see the next section). Everything downstream stays
> the same.

```{r simulate}
set.seed(100)

n_persons <- 400L
n_weeks   <- 40L
weeks     <- seq(as.Date("2024-01-01"), by = "week", length.out = n_weeks)

# ---- clearly-labelled illustrative effect ---------------------------------
# DEMO ONLY: this is the size of the behaviour change we inject into treated
# people after adoption. Set to 0 (or delete) when running on real data, so the
# model should estimate the effect, not have it baked in.
TREATMENT_EFFECT <- 0.8   # extra collaboration hours/week once adopted
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

persons <- tibble(
  PersonId    = sprintf("P%04d", seq_len(n_persons)),
  treated     = rbinom(n_persons, 1, 0.6),
  # person baseline (some people simply collaborate more than others)
  base_collab = rnorm(n_persons, mean = 12, sd = 3)
)

# Treated people adopt at a staggered week (10..28); controls never adopt.
persons <- persons %>%
  mutate(adopt_week = ifelse(
    treated == 1,
    sample(10:28, n_persons, replace = TRUE),
    NA_integer_
  ))

# calendar-week seasonality shared by everyone
week_shock <- tibble(
  week_idx  = seq_len(n_weeks),
  MetricDate = weeks,
  season    = 1.5 * sin(2 * pi * seq_len(n_weeks) / 26)
)

panel <- tidyr::crossing(PersonId = persons$PersonId, week_idx = seq_len(n_weeks)) %>%
  left_join(persons, by = "PersonId") %>%
  left_join(week_shock, by = "week_idx") %>%
  mutate(
    adopted_now = treated == 1 & week_idx >= adopt_week,
    # Copilot actions: 0 before adoption, positive afterwards (treated only)
    Total_Copilot_actions_taken = ifelse(
      adopted_now, rpois(n(), lambda = 25), 0L
    ),
    # primary outcome: baseline + season + injected effect (post-adoption) + noise
    Collaboration_hours = base_collab + season +
      ifelse(adopted_now, TREATMENT_EFFECT, 0) +
      rnorm(n(), 0, 2),
    # two correlated collaboration outcomes for the composite index later
    Chat_hours  = 0.35 * Collaboration_hours + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.8),
    Emails_sent = 20 + 1.2 * Collaboration_hours + rnorm(n(), 0, 4)
  ) %>%
  select(PersonId, MetricDate, week_idx, treated,
         Total_Copilot_actions_taken,
         Collaboration_hours, Chat_hours, Emails_sent)

head(panel)
```

## Derive the adoption week and event time

On a real export you would not know who is "treated"; you would infer it from
the data. Here we reproduce that realistic step: a person is an **adopter** if
they ever record a non-zero Copilot action, and their **adoption week** is the
first such week. Control people (never any actions) are assigned a **placebo**
adoption week (the median adopter week), so they contribute a comparable
event-time window.

```{r event-time}
adopt <- panel %>%
  filter(Total_Copilot_actions_taken > 0) %>%
  group_by(PersonId) %>%
  summarise(adopt_date = min(MetricDate), .groups = "drop")

# Calendar-week number and adoption cohort for the staggered-robust estimator.
# Never-adopters are coded 1000, a value outside the observed period range, which
# is how fixest::sunab() identifies the never-treated cohort.
NEVER <- 1000L
first_date <- min(panel$MetricDate)
panel <- panel %>%
  left_join(adopt, by = "PersonId") %>%
  mutate(
    is_adopter = !is.na(adopt_date),
    week_num   = as.integer((MetricDate - first_date) / 7) + 1L,
    cohort     = ifelse(is_adopter,
                        as.integer((adopt_date - first_date) / 7) + 1L,
                        NEVER)
  )

# Early adopters with no observed pre-period cannot contribute to an adoption
# estimate: they look like people treated for the whole window, so there is no
# "before" to compare with (see the "check pre-adoption" section of
# https://microsoft.github.io/viva-insights-sample-code/articles/causal-questions-ai-usage/#check-pre-adoption ).
# Drop people with fewer than MIN_PRE observed pre-adoption weeks.
MIN_PRE <- 4L
early <- panel %>%
  filter(is_adopter) %>%
  group_by(PersonId) %>%
  summarise(n_pre = sum(week_num < cohort), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n_pre < MIN_PRE)
cat(sprintf(
  "Dropped %d people who adopted with fewer than %d observed pre-adoption weeks (no usable 'before').\n",
  nrow(early), MIN_PRE
))
panel <- panel %>% filter(!PersonId %in% early$PersonId)

adopt <- filter(adopt, !PersonId %in% early$PersonId)
placebo_date <- as.Date(median(adopt$adopt_date))

panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(
    anchor     = dplyr::coalesce(adopt_date, placebo_date),
    event_week = as.integer((MetricDate - anchor) / 7)
  )

# Keep a balanced +/- 8-week window around each person's anchor
# (used for the naive TWFE comparison only)
WINDOW <- 8L
panel_es <- panel %>%
  filter(event_week >= -WINDOW, event_week <= WINDOW) %>%
  group_by(PersonId) %>%
  filter(sum(event_week < 0) >= 4, sum(event_week > 0) >= 4) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    treated_grp = as.integer(is_adopter),
    post        = as.integer(event_week >= 0),
    treat_post  = post * treated_grp
  )

panel_es %>%
  distinct(PersonId, treated_grp) %>%
  count(group = ifelse(treated_grp == 1, "Adopter (treated)", "Non-adopter (control)"))
```

## Primary estimate: Sun and Abraham interaction-weighted event study

The estimator fits a coefficient for every adoption cohort $g$ and calendar
week, relative to the week before adoption (event time -1), with never-adopters
as the comparison group:

$$y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \sum_{g}\sum_{\ell \ne -1} \delta_{g,\ell}\,\mathbf{1}\{G_i = g\}\,\mathbf{1}\{t - g = \ell\} + \varepsilon_{it}$$

where $\alpha_i$ are person fixed effects, $\gamma_t$ are calendar-week fixed
effects, and standard errors are clustered by person. The cohort-specific
coefficients are then averaged, weighted by cohort share, to give one effect per
event week. In `fixest` this is the `sunab(cohort, period)` term. It uses the
full panel, because the estimator compares each cohort with never-adopters in
calendar time and needs no placebo adoption week.

```{r sunab}
es_sa <- fixest::feols(
  Collaboration_hours ~ sunab(cohort, week_num, ref.p = -1) | PersonId + week_num,
  data    = panel,
  cluster = ~PersonId
)

# Average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), averaged over post-adoption weeks
summary(es_sa, agg = "ATT")

att <- coeftable(es_sa, agg = "ATT")
cat(sprintf(
  "\nSun-Abraham ATT estimate: %+.2f collaboration hours/week (SE %.2f; injected demo effect was %+.2f)\n",
  att[1, "Estimate"], att[1, "Std. Error"], TREATMENT_EFFECT
))
```

The estimate should land close to the injected `TREATMENT_EFFECT`. On real data
you would not know the true value, and the estimate depends on the assumptions
listed above.

## The event-study: look at pre-trends and see the estimate emerge

A single average hides the **parallel-trends** assumption. The event-study
version shows a separate estimate for each event week (relative to week -1). If
the design is credible, the **pre-adoption** estimates should sit near zero, and
the **post-adoption** estimates should step up to the effect.

```{r event-study, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
# Event-time estimates aggregated across cohorts (one per relative week)
es_tab <- as.data.frame(coeftable(es_sa))
es_tab$term <- rownames(es_tab)
es_coefs <- es_tab %>%
  filter(grepl("^week_num::", term)) %>%
  mutate(
    event_week = as.integer(sub("^week_num::(-?\\d+).*", "\\1", term)),
    lwr = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std. Error`,
    upr = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std. Error`
  ) %>%
  filter(event_week >= -WINDOW, event_week <= WINDOW)

# Add the reference week (-1) at exactly 0
es_coefs <- bind_rows(
  es_coefs,
  tibble(event_week = -1, Estimate = 0, lwr = 0, upr = 0)
) %>% arrange(event_week)

ggplot(es_coefs, aes(event_week, Estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "#5fa8d3", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#1b4965") +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#1b4965") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-WINDOW, WINDOW, 2)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Event-study (Sun and Abraham): collaboration hours around Copilot adoption",
    subtitle = "Estimates vs event week (ref = week -1), 95% CI, never-adopters as comparison.",
    x = "Weeks relative to adoption", y = "Estimate vs week -1 (hours/week)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### Pre-trend check

A joint Wald test on the pre-adoption estimates in the plotted window (event
weeks -8 to -2, excluding the reference week -1) asks whether they are jointly
different from zero. The averaging weights are rebuilt from the cohort-specific
coefficients, so the test uses the same person-clustered covariance as the plot.

```{r pretrend}
b  <- es_sa$coefficients
V  <- vcov(es_sa)
mm <- model.matrix(es_sa)
leads <- -WINDOW:-2

# Weights that average cohort-specific coefficients into one estimate per lead
A <- t(sapply(leads, function(l) {
  w  <- numeric(length(b))
  nm <- grep(sprintf("^week_num::%d:cohort::", l), names(b))
  n_obs <- colSums(sign(mm[, names(b)[nm], drop = FALSE]))
  w[nm] <- n_obs / sum(n_obs)
  w
}))

lead_est <- as.numeric(A %*% b)
wald_chi <- as.numeric(t(lead_est) %*% solve(A %*% V %*% t(A)) %*% lead_est)
cat(sprintf("Joint test of %d pre-adoption leads: chi-squared = %.2f, p = %.3f\n",
            length(leads), wald_chi,
            pchisq(wald_chi, df = length(leads), lower.tail = FALSE)))
```

A non-significant pre-test does not establish parallel trends. The test can
have low power, and it cannot rule out a trend that starts at adoption. Read it
together with the plot, and with what you know about why people adopted when
they did.

## Comparison: naive TWFE (shown for comparison)

For comparison only, the block below fits the single-coefficient TWFE DiD and
the TWFE event study that many analyses start with. With staggered adoption and
possibly different effects by cohort, these can be contaminated, so treat them
as a sensitivity check against the Sun and Abraham estimate above, not as the
headline. They use the +/- 8-week window around each person's anchor, with a
placebo anchor for controls.

```{r twfe}
did <- fixest::feols(
  Collaboration_hours ~ treat_post | PersonId + MetricDate,
  data    = panel_es,
  cluster = ~PersonId
)

summary(did)

did_beta <- coef(did)[["treat_post"]]
cat(sprintf(
  "\nNaive TWFE DiD estimate: %+.2f collaboration hours/week (injected demo effect was %+.2f)\n",
  did_beta, TREATMENT_EFFECT
))
```

```{r twfe-event-study, fig.width=9, fig.height=5}
es_twfe <- fixest::feols(
  Collaboration_hours ~ i(event_week, treated_grp, ref = -1) |
    PersonId + MetricDate,
  data    = panel_es,
  cluster = ~PersonId
)

tw_tab <- as.data.frame(coeftable(es_twfe))
tw_tab$term <- rownames(tw_tab)
tw_coefs <- tw_tab %>%
  filter(grepl("event_week::", term)) %>%
  mutate(
    event_week = as.integer(sub(".*event_week::(-?\\d+).*", "\\1", term)),
    lwr = Estimate - 1.96 * `Std. Error`,
    upr = Estimate + 1.96 * `Std. Error`
  )
tw_coefs <- bind_rows(
  tw_coefs,
  tibble(event_week = -1, Estimate = 0, lwr = 0, upr = 0)
) %>% arrange(event_week)

ggplot(tw_coefs, aes(event_week, Estimate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lwr, ymax = upr), fill = "#bc4b51", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, colour = "#bc4b51") +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#bc4b51") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(-WINDOW, WINDOW, 2)) +
  labs(
    title    = "Naive TWFE event-study (shown for comparison)",
    subtitle = "Estimates vs event week (ref = week -1), 95% CI.",
    x = "Weeks relative to adoption", y = "Estimate vs week -1 (hours/week)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## Bonus: run the same design on a composite index

Individual metrics can be noisy. One option is to combine several
related collaboration metrics into a single **z-scored composite index**, then
run the same Sun and Abraham estimate on the index. Each component is standardised across the
panel (mean 0, sd 1) and averaged, so no single metric's scale dominates.

```{r composite, fig.width=9, fig.height=4}
components <- c("Collaboration_hours", "Chat_hours", "Emails_sent")

zscore <- function(x) (x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)

panel <- panel %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(components), zscore, .names = "z_{.col}")) %>%
  mutate(collab_index = rowMeans(across(starts_with("z_")), na.rm = TRUE))

panel_es <- panel_es %>%
  left_join(select(panel, PersonId, MetricDate, collab_index),
            by = c("PersonId", "MetricDate"))

es_index <- fixest::feols(
  collab_index ~ sunab(cohort, week_num, ref.p = -1) | PersonId + week_num,
  data    = panel,
  cluster = ~PersonId
)

summary(es_index, agg = "ATT")

# Event-time trajectory of the composite, treated vs control
idx_traj <- panel_es %>%
  mutate(grp = ifelse(treated_grp == 1, "Adopter", "Control")) %>%
  group_by(grp, event_week) %>%
  summarise(idx = mean(collab_index), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(idx_traj, aes(event_week, idx, colour = grp)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Adopter" = "#1b4965", "Control" = "#bc4b51"),
                      name = NULL) +
  labs(
    title    = "Composite collaboration index around adoption",
    subtitle = "Mean z-scored index (Collaboration hours + Chat hours + Emails sent)",
    x = "Weeks relative to adoption", y = "Composite index (z-units)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

## Wrapping up

The Sun and Abraham event-study is a portable way to ask *"did behaviour
change after adoption, within the same person?"* while allowing for the fact
that adopters differ from non-adopters and adopt at different times. To apply it
to your own data, replace the simulation chunk with
`vivainsights::import_query()`, derive the adoption week from the first non-zero
Copilot action, set `TREATMENT_EFFECT` aside entirely, and let the model
estimate the effect. Inspect the pre-adoption estimates, compare against the
naive TWFE result, and remember that the output is an estimate under
assumptions. People who adopt Copilot choose to do so, so treat any estimate as
an association unless the design justifies more.
